mcqs.question: A screen reader is announcing a page. What is it actually reading from?
options: The page's CSS, to determine what looks interactive
The rendered pixels, using an OCR-like process
The accessibility tree — a role/name/state structure the browser computes from the DOM — queried through the OS accessibility API
The raw HTML source file directly, before the browser parses it
mcqs.explanation: Screen readers query the accessibility tree via the operating system's accessibility API; that tree is computed from the DOM's semantic meaning, not from visual styling, rendered pixels, or the raw unparsed source. This is exactly why visual-only fixes never help a screen reader user — the tool never touches that layer.

mcqs.question: A card component is built entirely from `<div>` elements, including a `<div onclick>` styled as a button. What does the accessibility tree contain for that clickable div?
options: A button role with no accessible name
A generic container role with a disabled state
A link role, since divs default to link behavior when given an onclick handler
Nothing interactive at all — divs contribute no role by default regardless of any click handler attached to them
mcqs.explanation: A div carries no default accessible role no matter what JS behavior is attached to it — onclick is invisible to the accessibility tree, so the element contributes no interactive node at all, not a button, a link, or even a disabled state. This is precisely why a div-as-button looks fine visually while being functionally absent for assistive tech.

mcqs.question: To make a `<div onclick>` behave like a real `<button>` for keyboard and screen-reader users, what has to be added manually?
options: role="button", tabindex="0", and a keydown handler for both Enter and Space, none of which a real button needs
Only a role="button" attribute — the browser infers the rest automatically
Nothing — modern browsers detect onclick handlers and infer button behavior
Only a CSS cursor: pointer style, which signals interactivity to assistive tech
mcqs.explanation: None of a button's native behaviors are inferred by browsers for a styled div — role, focusability, and key handling all have to be manually reimplemented and kept in sync, none of which a real <button> element requires since it gets all of it for free. Cursor styling is purely visual and has no effect on the accessibility tree.

mcqs.question: A page is built entirely from visually-styled `<div>`s instead of `<header>`, `<nav>`, `<main>`, and `<footer>`. What capability does a screen reader user specifically lose?
options: The ability to jump directly between landmark regions, forcing them to read or tab through the entire page linearly every time
The ability to zoom the page at all
The ability to read any text content on the page
The ability to submit any forms present on the page
mcqs.explanation: Landmark elements are what let a screen reader user jump straight to main content, skipping repeated navigation on every page load — losing them means falling back to linear reading or tabbing through everything, every time. Text content itself, zoom behavior, and form submission are unrelated to landmark presence.

mcqs.question: Converting a nav built from `<div onclick>` items into `<nav>` wrapping real `<a href>` elements changes the visual appearance how much?
options: Significantly — semantic elements require different CSS approaches that change the visual result
Not at all in terms of achievable styling — the same CSS properties apply to both, while gaining landmark role, focusability, and correct semantics for free
It removes the ability to style the links with custom colors or hover states
It requires abandoning any custom layout in favor of default browser styling
mcqs.explanation: Semantic elements accept the same CSS as generic ones — nothing about switching from div to nav/a restricts styling — so the fix is free in terms of visual flexibility while gaining a real landmark role and native keyboard behavior. None of the other options describe an actual constraint of using semantic markup.

mcqs.question: A "clickable anywhere" card is implemented as `<div class="card" onclick="navigate()">` containing its own internal link and button. What's the safest fix to make the whole card clickable while staying accessible?
options: Add role="button" to the outer div and nothing else
Wrap the entire card, including its nested link and button, in one outer <a href>
Leave the div as-is and add an aria-label describing that the card is clickable

Make the primary click target (often the title) a real <a href>, and use a CSS technique to keep the whole card visually clickable without nesting interactive elements inside another interactive element
mcqs.explanation: Wrapping the whole card in one outer link while it contains its own nested link/button creates invalid, confusing nested-interactive-element markup; the safer pattern makes one real link the actual interactive target and uses CSS to extend its clickable area visually. An aria-label alone doesn't add keyboard focusability or a real interactive role, and role="button" alone still misses tabindex and key handling.
